opus-5.5.text:
I think it starts with a kind of humility. A lot of us in AI research spend our days looking at benchmarks, loss curves, leaderboards, and it's very easy to forget that the real world doesn't look like ImageNet or a curated text corpus. People's everyday lives are messy, continuous, multimodal. You're cooking dinner while a kid is asking you a question and your phone is buzzing. That's the actual environment intelligence has to operate in.

So for me, understanding everyday life matters in two ways. First, as a research direction: if you watch how people actually move through the world, you realize so much of what we do isn't language. It's spatial, visual, physical. We remember where we put our keys, we predict what will happen if we nudge a cup off the table. That's part of why I care so much about visual understanding and world models. Language models are amazing, but they capture only a slice of human experience. If we want AI that's genuinely useful in daily life, it has to see and understand the physical world the way we do.

Second, on the product side, I think the best AI products won't feel like "AI products" at all. They'll disappear into the background of life. The question shouldn't be "what can this model do that's impressive in a demo?" but "where in someone's day is there friction, anxiety, or wasted time, and can we quietly remove it?" That requires actually observing people, talking to them, not just assuming that because a capability exists, people want it.

And honestly, there's a responsibility aspect too. Everyday life is intimate. If an AI is going to sit in your home, see what you see, hear your conversations, then trust becomes the core product feature. Understanding people's lives means understanding their boundaries, not just their needs.

So I'd say: let real life set the agenda, rather than letting the technology set the agenda and then searching for a use case afterward.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes humility and understanding everyday life, but does not say that loving life is a prerequisite for making a good product.

r002.rationale: It says product decisions should start from real-life friction and people’s actual wants, and that real life should set the agenda rather than technology.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think this is actually one of the questions that gets overlooked the most in our field, because so much of the energy goes into benchmarks and leaderboards, and relatively little goes into asking what people actually do with their days.

My own view comes partly from how I think about vision research. Vision is interesting precisely because it is grounded in the physical world. Language models can get very far by consuming text, but text is already a compressed, curated description of life. When you look at images or video, you're looking at the raw, messy, unedited version of how people actually live. A parent's kitchen at 7 a.m., a construction site, a hospital corridor. None of that shows up in the kind of data that gets written down. So if you only build from what people have bothered to write, you inherit a very skewed picture of what matters.

That's why I think product development should start from observation rather than from capability. The typical pattern right now is: we have a model that can do X, so let's find a use case for X. That's backwards. The better question is: where do people spend time, where do they get frustrated, where do they repeat themselves, and is there something a model could absorb there? Often the answer is something unglamorous. It's not writing a poem. It's noticing that someone takes the same photo of a receipt every week and hates it.

There's a second point I'd make, which is about understanding the gap between demos and daily use. A demo is thirty seconds in ideal conditions. Daily life is a thousand small interactions under bad lighting, with partial information, with people who are distracted. A model that works brilliantly in the demo but fails ten percent of the time in the field is, from the user's point of view, unreliable. And unreliability is what kills products. So understanding everyday life also means understanding the long tail, the edge cases that are actually the median case once you leave the lab.

I also think there's a cultural dimension that gets flattened. Everyday life in Shanghai, in a small town in Ohio, in Jakarta, these are genuinely different, and the assumptions baked into a product reflect wherever the team happened to be sitting. When I look at the training data for a lot of visual systems, it's enormously biased toward certain environments and certain kinds of objects. If you want AI to be useful to a broad population, you have to go and look at how a broad population actually lives, not infer it from the internet.

And finally, I think understanding people should also set limits on what we build. Not everything that can be automated should be. Some parts of daily life people value doing themselves, even if they're inefficient. A good product respects that. The goal isn't to replace living, it's to remove the friction around it so people have more room for the parts that matter to them. That's a judgment you can only make if you've actually paid attention to what those parts are.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes observing everyday life and respecting what people value, but it does not say that loving life is a prerequisite for making a good product.

r002.rationale: It says product development should start by observing where people spend time, feel frustrated, or repeat tasks, and then ask whether a model could help there.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with what people actually do every day. Where do they spend their time? What frustrates them? What do they care about enough that they would change a habit? Those questions should shape the product, rather than starting with a model capability and looking for somewhere to put it.

For example, someone might ask AI to help write an email, but the hard part may not be writing. It might be deciding how to say no without damaging a relationship. If you only see the task as text generation, you miss a lot of what that person needs.

So I think observing people and listening to them is essential. And then you have to put the product into their lives and see whether it actually helps. Does it save effort, or does checking its work become another chore? Can people understand when to trust it? A very impressive demo can still fail those everyday tests. Understanding that gap is a big part of building something useful.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes observing and listening to people, but does not present loving life as a prerequisite for making a good product.

r002.rationale: It says people’s everyday activities, frustrations, and priorities should shape the product instead of starting with a model capability and searching for a use. That communicates that AI should be introduced based on people’s needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should start by understanding what people actually do every day—where they spend time, what frustrates them, and what they care about. If we start only from what a model can do, it’s easy to build an impressive demo that doesn’t solve a meaningful problem.

And everyday life is messy. People don’t always know how to describe what they need, and they shouldn’t have to become experts at prompting to get something useful. Watching how people use a product, where they hesitate, and where they correct it can teach us a lot.

That should guide both the product and the research. Sometimes the most valuable improvement isn’t a more elaborate answer; it’s knowing when to ask a question, being reliable, or fitting naturally into something someone already does. The goal is to make people’s lives easier, and we have to judge that in their actual lives.

r001.rationale: The response advocates understanding everyday life and making people’s lives easier, but does not present loving life as a prerequisite for making a good product.

r002.rationale: It says everyday needs should guide product development, but does not state that those needs should determine whether to introduce AI into a product.
